articles.summary: An independent Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon franchisee cut menu repricing time by 95% and built a workflow that could free up $100K in cash flow.

Title: Franchisee reconciles cash in 94% less time with ChatGPT Work

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/ted-taylor-restaurant

Markdown Content:
Ted Taylor entered the restaurant business after a 25-year career in the semiconductor industry. Today, he’s an independent franchisee operating three co-branded Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon restaurants across New Mexico.

Running quick-service restaurants means balancing the customer experience with a lot of work customers never see, like menu pricing, staffing, equipment maintenance, and policies. Ted uses OpenAI technology to get through all of it faster.

With ChatGPT, Ted accelerates time-consuming tasks like research and drafting, and he uses ChatGPT Work to gather and analyze volumes of data across pricing, sales, forecasts, schedules, and labor and to get recommendations on where each restaurant needs attention, reducing repricing time by 95% and shaving 4 hours off payroll runs.

> “ChatGPT Work’s recommendations are so good that it’s much faster to start there and then make adjustments.”

—Ted Taylor, independent franchisee, Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon

## Repricing menus across three markets in minutes

Repricing menus is an annual undertaking that requires a complex analysis of recipe costs, item popularity, local competitor pricing, portion sizes, and the different economics of in-store and delivery orders. Ted uses ChatGPT Work to bring those factors together and get pricing recommendations in 1 - 2 hours instead of 5 days.

> “It used to take me a few days of work to analyze and come up with item-level pricing; whereas, ChatGPT Work tears through it in a matter of moments and does it more thoroughly.”

—Ted Taylor, independent franchisee, Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon

Ted first uses ChatGPT Work to research and establish his pricing targets and pricing strategies based on local competitors’ pricing trends, portion sizes, and relative food quality. He then gives ChatGPT Work a categorized list of menu items with their current in-store and delivery prices. He specifies how much he wants each set of prices to increase overall and which items should receive larger or smaller increases, largely based on the earlier analysis from ChatGPT.

He can make the analysis more detailed by adding item-level sales history and supplier prices. ChatGPT Work can use these inputs to estimate sales impacts from price changes and to optimize item-level pricing around cost of goods targets.

ChatGPT Work returns a spreadsheet with recommended in-store and delivery prices. It will even relate the pricing changes to an overall pricing strategy designed to optimize business outcomes like customer retention, minimizing price shocks, and best positioning of add-ons.

The first time Ted used ChatGPT Work for pricing, he also ran the analysis manually. “ChatGPT Work made a deeper local comparison and helped me avoid increases that would have made some items uncompetitive,” he said. Ted immediately switched to using ChatGPT to develop the first recommendations.

## Finding ways to optimize labor and free up cash flow

Ted uses ChatGPT Work to help manage labor costs in two ways: reviewing how labor is tracking across his three restaurants and testing a better way to build the weekly schedule.

For the labor analysis, Ted gave ChatGPT Work read-only access to his sales and labor data. When he runs the analysis, it compares scheduled, budgeted, and actual hours with forecast and actual sales. It also reviews the previous 12 weeks to account for stores that routinely come in above or below their sales forecasts. The resulting report flags overtime, shifts running longer than planned, and gaps in coverage, and highlights what a manager should review.

For the scheduling test, Ted gave ChatGPT Work an employee roster with each person’s role, training, availability, and pay, along with the store’s staffing needs at different sales levels. He and the manager compared ChatGPT Work’s proposed schedule with what she would have built, identified missing rules about when to add staff during busy periods, and refined the instructions for ChatGPT Work.

ChatGPT Work now produces a full schedule for that location. The manager checks it over, makes adjustments if needed, and enters it into the restaurant’s scheduling system. Ted estimates that better scheduling could eventually reduce hourly labor costs by one to two percentage points of sales across all three restaurants, which could add $50,000 to $100,000 in free cash flow annually that can be utilized for increased pay, bonuses, investment in the business, or increased profit distributions.

## Accelerating back-office tasks with ChatGPT Work

Ted also uses ChatGPT Work for day-to-day operations, from developing HR policies to reconciling cash and managing supply and repair requests.

When New Mexico started requiring restaurants to keep a written procedure for bodily-fluid incidents, Ted used ChatGPT to write a draft in about 30 seconds. When Ted needed a social media policy for his employee handbook, ChatGPT helped him quickly draft guidance that an outside HR firm later reviewed without making any changes.

Ted uses ChatGPT Work to reconcile cash monthly across his three restaurants. He uploads each store’s cash transaction data and bank records, and ChatGPT Work compares the transactions with the corresponding deposits. Monthly reconciliation used to take three hours, and now it takes 5-10 minutes. He also cut four hours of manual work from every payroll cycle by using ChatGPT Work to summarize payroll inputs.

To help keep restaurants running smoothly, Ted also used ChatGPT Work to build a web portal where employees can request supplies or repairs. The portal notifies him through a dedicated email address and tracks each request’s status.

## More time to improve the business, not just run it

Ted’s approach to using ChatGPT Work is practical for any small-business owner. He gives ChatGPT the same data and guidelines he’d use to make a decision and compares its output with how he’d do the work himself. As he gains confidence in the results, he expands his use to more tasks around the business, always reviewing the results before implementing.

For Ted, the value of ChatGPT Work goes beyond hours saved. Now he can do analysis he might otherwise skip and spend more time on customers, employees, and growing the business.

# Spain-Based Startups Advance Regional Innovation With Barcelona Supercomputing Center

 Part of NVIDIA Inception and the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme, the companies are advancing technologies for healthcare providers, utilities and more.

October 19, 2026 by[Tobias Halloran](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/thalloran/ "Posts by Tobias Halloran")

 Share

Share This Article

The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC)’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries.

Many of these companies are also members of the [NVIDIA Inception](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/startups/) program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some of the BSC AI Factory services are available through the NVIDIA Inception portal.

NVIDIA Inception complements the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme by providing members with training through [NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/training/) open courses, business mentoring, venture capital connections and other resources.

An upcoming extension of MareNostrum 5 — BSC’s public infrastructure serving scientific and technological innovation, powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing — will deliver supercomputing access through the BSC AI Factory and other AI Factories across Europe. BSC AI Factory is among Europe’s first AI factories and the first in Spain, and has delivered more than 800 services to private and public-sector clients since its April 2025 launch.

Three Inception members were recently named the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme’s AI Champions at the pilot initiative’s demo day:

**Qatium**’s water-network platform — already used by more than 250 utilities in 16 countries — is now in early production with its Neural Water Intelligence technology, powered by proprietary AI models trained on MareNostrum 5. Built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, the [NVIDIA cuGraph](https://github.com/rapidsai/cugraph) library, the [NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo](https://developer.nvidia.com/physicsnemo) framework and [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) open models, the technology helps water utilities make better operational decisions every day.

**OneCareAI**, a research spin-off from BSC, used [NVIDIA NIM](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/products/nim-microservices/) microservices to develop technology designed to identify signs of hidden atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm — in seemingly normal ECGs, helping clinicians identify patients who may be at risk of stroke before one occurs.

**Avatia** built a voice-first, multi-agent system that provides pharmaceutical companies with agentic coworkers that support sales representatives and give doctors transparent, curated information about medicines, ultimately helping the right treatment reach the right patient sooner. The system taps into NVIDIA NIM microservices, the [NVIDIA Nemotron 3](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) open model family and the open source [NVIDIA NeMo Curator](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Curator) library.

Other BSC AI Factory startups — Agrikola AI, Elna Health, Lokutor, Montevive AI, Oppy, Pack2Earth and Up2Smart — span precision agriculture, medical imaging and knowledge access, speech services, enterprise security, sales intelligence and sustainable packaging.

The cohort reflects the breadth of what advanced intelligence can now unlock: preventing strokes, detecting breast cancer subtypes before biopsy, putting medical knowledge at doctors’ fingertips faster, replacing petroleum-based plastic with biobased compostable materials, protecting crops with robots instead of chemicals and more.

articles.title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
articles.summary: The proposed policy seems to offer protections against AI run amok but actually forbids federal agencies from blocking a model's release without the permission of a judge.
articles.content:
Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry.
Politico
recently reported
that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution.
Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes.
The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law,
Senate Bill 53
, which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”
Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes.
It’s not clear how this proposed system would assure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that
a self-governing AI regulatory body should
mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).
In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to  request to a D.C. judge to halt the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s a request for comment but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in
Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework
, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said.
The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there
are people warning of the potential
of human death, the primary concern has largely been the
threat of agentic hacking
. A
rash of incidents
in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls.
In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions.
Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of
embedded evaluators
— supposedly “neutral” third-party observers that are placed inside AI organizations so that they can monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse.
Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, who’s CEO Jensen Huang recently
argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all.

articles.title: Hugging Face CEO warns that Netflix’s OpenAI hack documentary isn’t accurate
articles.summary: Before you share the Netflix documentary "AI Gone Rogue" take note. Clem Delangue, Hugging Face's co-founder who is featured in the film, says it went "full doomer mode" and isn't accurate.
articles.content:
Before you share the Netflix documentary “AI Gone Rogue” with family or friends to help them understand why the AI industry freaked out so badly that
leaders called for a slowdown
, take note: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, says the film isn’t accurate. He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the
famed attack
on his company by rogue OpenAI agents.
“Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode,” Delangue
wrote in a post on X.
“I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.”
To be fair, the documentary does have experts who
explained what happened fairly well
, including Delangue himself and Ryan Greenblatt, the researcher at METR who helped investigate and co-authored the report on what happened.
In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment,
spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face
as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given. The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize. The incident stemmed from a lack of
proper security safeguards
and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible.
But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack.
In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.”
Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.”
But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers.
The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack.
But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote.
It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on screen.
Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!”
In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take.

articles.title: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
articles.summary: SpaceX hit profitably in the third-quarter, with net income of $4.4 billion. AI was the engine.
articles.content:
SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.
CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its
regulatory filing
.
That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.
The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.
The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.
During a live-streamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online.
“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”
In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12 to 18 month delays in obtaining the metals blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly.
Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.
SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity.
Despite of those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.
Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”
More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion.
This is a developing story. TechCrunch will update.

articles.title: Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia’s stronghold with AI app developers
articles.summary: Google has joined Amazon in releasing a developer tool that makes it easy for PyTorch users to move their apps off Nvidia GPUs.
articles.content:
On Tuesday, Google
announced
that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open-source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to
break Nvidia’s stranglehold
on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs.
PyTorch is the popular open-source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects.
Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no re-writing of their apps.
Amazon made a
similar announcement Monday,
when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting. Amazon also said it going even further in its effort to loosen Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch. It is submitting code to the main PyTorch project that decouples various features from Nvidia’s chips, making it more open to any hardware by default.
Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however. It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM) RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does.
Plus the search giant has launched a dedicated tool, the
TPU agent suite
, to help developers move their apps to Google’s chips and cloud and fix errors along the way. It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps.
None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage.

articles.title: ChatGPT now lets you lock your chats
articles.summary: The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat.
articles.content:
OpenAI
announced
on Tuesday that users can now lock ChatGPT conversations to keep sensitive chats private when others may have access to their screen or device. Users can secure their locked chats with a four-digit PIN, or use Face ID or Touch ID on supported devices.
Unlike the app’s Temporary Chats, which provide a separate session that doesn’t appear in chat history, users can return to Locked Chats at any time.
The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat.
The addition of locked chats adds a new layer of privacy to ChatGPT, as the app is increasingly used for
personal conversations
. Of course, while locking a chat can limit access, it doesn’t address concerns about how sensitive information is stored or handled.
OpenAI notes that locking a chat doesn’t create end-to-end encryption or a separate encrypted vault, change how long it retains the chat, remove information that ChatGPT remembered before a chat was locked, or change the “Improve the model for everyone” setting.
Once users lock a chat, it moves to a dedicated “Locked Chats” section, where it’s kept separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and chat search results.
With Memory enabled, Locked Chats has its own separate memory shared across conversations within the section. New messages sent after locking a chat can update that memory, but don’t update regular Memory. That means new information from locked chats won’t leak into regular chats.
OpenAI says resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN.
Additionally, the Locked Chats option isn’t available for temporary chats, archived chats, group chats, chats created from a shared link, chats with scheduled tasks, and chats with meeting recordings.
Locked Chats
will be available to users on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans. The company notes that the feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare. The feature is starting to roll out on Tuesday, so it may not be live yet for all users.

articles.title: Meta’s Muse hits 10M U.S. downloads in 40 days, a milestone reached by only 11 other apps
articles.summary: Meta's AI companion Muse has surpassed 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days, joining an exclusive group of apps that includes Threads. New data also shows Muse is retaining users at higher rates than its AI rivals.
articles.content:
Meta’s AI companion,
Muse, is now one of only a dozen mobile apps to have reached 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. According to new data from market intelligence provider
Sensor Tower,
Muse has seen 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of which were in the United States.
Only 11 other apps to date have reached this type of post-launch milestone, said Sensor Tower’s Senior Insights Analyst Kara Lee. The most recent of these was Meta’s Threads, back in July 2023.
Other apps that saw this kind of scale were largely mobile games, Lee noted, like Fortnite, PUBG Mobile, Pokémon GO, and others. Besides Threads, Disney+ was the only other non-game app to make it into the exclusive club.
Meta’s success is tied to the company’s
ability to scale its new apps
by marketing them across its other services, which it has done with both
Threads
and Muse. Threads was built on top of Instagram’s social graph, and its content has been
integrated
into both Facebook and Instagram. However, Muse isn’t only benefiting from Meta’s ability to market the AI agent across its family of apps, which today includes 3.6 billion daily active users; the company is also heavily investing in advertising to drive new users to Muse.
Per Sensor Tower’s data, Meta has allocated 39% of its total advertising spend to market Muse in October, up from 23% last month. In addition, Muse now ranks as the 21st largest brand in the U.S. by advertising impressions this month, up from 73rd in September.
Still, marketing an app and retaining users after the initial shine wears off are two different things. In this case, Muse is seeing better retention rates than its AI competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok.
In the U.S., the app had a 30% retention rate after 7 days and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. By comparison, its rivals saw an average of a 19% 7-day retention rate and a 16% 14-day retention rate, according to the firm’s data.
Muse also hit another milestone that demonstrates active engagement with the AI app. Its daily active users reached 2.5 million for the first time on October 16, a 15% week-over-week increase.
Meta’s latest AI app, which can handle various tasks on users’ behalf, has seen
breakout success
since its debut. It shot up to No. 1 on the App Store, and, at one point, even
outpaced some of the metrics
ChatGPT saw following its launch. Its latest milestone sees it topping its rivals again, as ChatGPT saw 3.7 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. Grok and Claude saw only 500,000 and 200,000 U.S. downloads, respectively, in their first 40 days.
Globally, ChatGPT beat out Muse, having scaled to around 15 million global downloads in its first 40 days. But this isn’t a fair comparison, as ChatGPT benefited from a wider reach. Muse is only available in the U.S. and Canada for now, while ChatGPT’s app attracted attention from markets like Japan, Brazil, and Germany, too. (Japan, for instance, accounted for 25% of its global installs during its first 40 days.)
Since launching, Muse has retained its No. 1 rank on the U.S. App Store for all days except October 19, when streaming app Kick briefly beat it out. It has since reclaimed the top spot as of Tuesday. Muse has also been No. 1 on Google Play over the past 30 days.

articles.title: Plants can speak using electricity, so this startup built an AI model to decipher their language
articles.summary: Electric Plant has built an AI-powered translator to help humans listen to what plants are saying with the subtle electricity coursing through their stems.
articles.content:
Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant.
A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a
houseplant wired to a motorized stand
. When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source.
“I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.”
Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found
Electric Plant
, which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers.
Electric Plant co-founders Lee von Kraus (right) and Justin Mast stand next to a tree with a sensor attached to it.
Image Credits:
Electric Plant
The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant.
To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised an $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song.
Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers, and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients, or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said.
“That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said.
Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said.
The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said.
The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network.
Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more.
Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry.
Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods, and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said.
“This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.”

articles.title: Figma co-founder Dylan Field thinks MCP is not a perfect protocol
articles.summary: Figma said it plans to support as many standards as possible without exposing all of its data.
articles.content:
Despite Figma co-founder Dylan Field’s concerns about MCP (model context protocol), which standardizes how AI agents connect to external data sources and tools, the company is expanding its support for the open source standard.
At the design company’s first Config conference held in India, the company announced 20 new MCP partners, including Amp, ClickUp, Dia, Junie by JetBrains, Linear, Meta Muse, Mistral, Notion, OpenCode, and Sarvam Agents.
Field has expressed his misgivings about MCP before. Days before this announcement, one of MCP’s co-creators complained about Figma not supporting the open source tool Pi. As part of his response, Field made a comment about Anthropic not making its various resources available via MCP.
“I find it interesting that Anthropic (creators of MCP standard) do not expose artifacts/other cloud resources created via MCP,” he wrote on X. “The debate is framed as open vs closed. Everyone always prefers open … obviously. And meanwhile issues of asymmetric context sharing are ignored.”
(Field later added that
Figma plans support Pi.
)
Can you help me understand why you don't make various Anthropic resources available via MCP? Maybe I'm missing something.
— Dylan Field (@zoink)
September 30, 2026
At a media briefing, I asked Field about this debate. The co-founder explained that while Figma wants to be open, he doesn’t think MCP is a perfect protocol.
“I’m really excited about what we’re doing in terms of opening up our ecosystem. I also think that MCP is not a perfect protocol. And I think that it is something that has tons of room for improvement,” the co-founder responded. “It is advantaged more to frontier labs. Also, I understand everyone online who just wants a protocol that they can use when they want to use their Figma data, and I want them to use it, too.”
Figma’s CEO said that the reason the company doesn’t want to be fully open is that the more data the company exposes through MCP, the higher the chance of abuse.
He also clarified that while most users don’t intend to use MCP or Figma data in a malicious way, the company still has to think about those potential risks.

articles.title: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
articles.summary: The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products and third-party services built using its technology, citing national security concerns.
articles.content:
The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup
DeepSeek
and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to
the Department of Homeland Security
. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, and
covers
third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions.
The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from U.S. government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said.
The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the U.S. and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models.
China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to
an offic
i
al briefing
. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added.
The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems.
Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks,
Bloomberg reported last week
.
The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the
globe
since its R1 reasoning model
shook the AI industry in
January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off of
Nvidia shares.
The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to
a September report.
In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year,
OpenAI
told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while
Anthropic
said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude.

articles.title: Eka is worth $1.45B thanks to a physical AI model that has experts raving
articles.summary: Eka Robotics may be the first robotic arm that is actually good at picking a wide range of objects up, and it is so smooth and human-like, it is wowing the industry.
articles.content:
Robots still aren’t that good at picking things up, despite billions of dollars of investment and endless videos fed into deep learning models.
That may be about to change, thanks to a manipulation architecture built by Eka Robotics, which encompasses a force-sensitive gripper and a new kind of deep-learning model. Founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, the startup just closed an $150 million Series A round that values it at $1.45 billion post-money, led by venture funds a16z and F-Prime.
“They are already exceeding superhuman performance for certain tasks, and so we think over the next few months there will be superhuman performance in many dexterous manipulation tasks,” Raghu Raghuram, the a16z general partner who co-led the fundraising round, told TechCrunch.
In an era of never-ending robotic demonstrations, Eka’s capabilities are shocking veteran robot builders.
Kris Hauser, a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said it had a “wow factor” compared to other robot demos he saw recently. The Eka robot “was able to adapt to a large number of different objects without retraining,” Hauser said, adding that it also had an aspect of “humanness, creepy humanness that it would try over and over again if it failed the first time.”
Another roboticist, who asked for anonymity because of their work at a frontier lab, told TechCrunch that seeing Eka’s robot in action was an emotional experience, comparable to when robots first achieved reliable legged locomotion five to ten years ago. Take a look for yourself:
Loading the player…
What’s notable here? How smoothly and rapidly the robot moves. It can pick up about 1,500 objects that weigh up to 1 kg in an hour, compared to about 600 for a human; Eka says it reliably picks up objects more than 95% of the time. And the robot arm is strong enough to hurt itself as it moves that quickly. That indicates, per the frontier lab observer, that “they have a lot of trust in their algorithm not breaking the robot. I wonder how many robots they broke along the way?”
When the frontier lab roboticist met Eka’s robot, they handed it a raspberry, the lab’s apparent favorite test item. “The experience of a big, heavy robot rushing towards my arm and then slowing down just in time and very gently touching me is a feeling that I am, as we speak, carrying this feeling in my body,” they told TechCrunch.
How not to squish the raspberry
These capabilities are a consequence of how the foundational model was built. Rather than a vision-language-action model — which is trained to understand the relationship between language, visual inputs, and actions — the schema here is a vision-force-action model, which focuses on the relationship between language, force inputs, and actions. Critics of the current direction of generative AI robotics models,
like Rodney Brooks
, say that they will fail without an attempt to represent force and touch; Eka’s results suggest such critics have a point.
“Vision is not the primary way in which you close this last millimeter problem,” Eka co-founder Agrawal told TechCrunch. “Vision tells you roughly where the object is, what the pose is, but the actual grabbing, the actual searching is happening through forces.”
Eka had to design a unique robotic hand that was more flexible than traditional grippers, and included more force sensors; it reacts to contact, which is why it doesn’t crush the raspberry. The founders are cagey about how they achieved that for obvious competitive reasons, but it comes down to using a physics simulator to model the multiple forces the robot will encounter as it attempts to grasp something, and using that to create a reinforcement learning environment that can be run at scale. They say they can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes.
“Rather than being limited to the data that you’re collecting from, say, human demonstrations, Eka is pushing through reinforcement learning this approach where the robot can surpass any kind of demonstrations that are given to it,” Hauser said. “What’s really exciting is that they’re able to not be limited to the data that is presented to them for training.”
Agrawal and Haarnoja, who first met in graduate school at the University of California, Berkeley, are leading researchers in the field of reinforcement learning for robotics control. Eka’s key bet was that this technique could be done at scale through simulation, rather than relying on videos collected by gigworkers or robot operators performing tasks over many hours. Simulation was key to achieving their robot’s reliable manipulation, a feat that in the past that has proven more difficult for tasks that require interacting with objects, rather than avoiding them.
“What EKA is bridging is the generality-performance gap, which plagues a lot of modern robotics,” Agrawal argues.
Making a general-purpose robot useful
Right now, the most generalizable physical AI models—the ones that can attempt lots of different tasks—aren’t
particularly good
at them. But AI models trained to be highly capable at a single task may not close the business case for a company: The promise of generative AI is that robots can quickly learn multiple tasks, even novel ones.
The current approaches are good at producing robots that are more generally intelligent than before — Astra, ChatGPT’s latest LLM, can
operate a robot
in an unfamiliar setting and perform tasks with it, but slowly and at a high cost. The promise of a model like Eka’s is that it handles the physicality while a more general model makes decisions about how to solve a problem. Astra, for example, might know that plates get stacked in a cupboard when they come out of the dishwasher, but Eka’s model is capable of picking up a dish without breaking it.
“Most of the field has been focusing on the planning,” Eka co-founder Haarnoja says, “so they approach from the top: high-level intelligence, pushing that down towards the physical. Whereas we think about it from the bottom up.”
Eka still needs to prove itself in the field, though. The company is working in secretive pilots with a number of industrial customers doing pick-and-place and wire manipulation, but the leap from lab to line is almost as big as the gap between sim and real.
“What’s going to be a big challenge is when they work with integrators on real assembly lines, and it needs to run without breaking for an entire year,” Hauser said. The other open question is “‘how generalizable these techniques can be to different tasks?’ What I’ve seen is pick and place, but many industry tasks that are value added involve more than just pick-and-place.”
Agrawal is also focused on deployability; right now, he says Eka’s gripper hardware — which costs less than $1,000 — is rated for 5 million duty cycles, but the ultimate goal is to hit the 20 million cycle bar set by standard industrial arms.
“What we are building is that engineering of how to design entire workflows, but we are starting off being very pragmatic, and saying here are two verticals in pick, arrange, place, and wire handling, let’s make them be home runs,” Agrawal said. “Once we have made home runs on them, the sky is the limit in how much we can do with the approach we are developing.”

articles.content:
Meeting note-taking tool
Otter.ai
announced on Tuesday that it has raised $320 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF), which provides capital to startups without diluting equity and gets returns on the results of marketing spend.
Otter.ai said that it will use these funds for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation.
The startup, which has been around for nearly a decade, has raised $50 million in total funding with its last round in 2021, according to PitchBook data.
Last year, Otter hit a revenue milestone after crossing
$100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR)
. The company said it’s now approaching new milestones, but didn’t provide updated figures.
The company said that 40 million users have used its product to date, up from 25 million last year. However, given the crowded space among meeting note-taking products, a pertinent challenge for Otter would be to have its customers stick around. Unfortunately, the startup didn’t provide any numbers around its monthly active users or churn.
“Voice is one of the biggest untapped opportunities in enterprise AI, and Otter is at the forefront of it – a conviction that’s only deepened watching Otter’s growth,” said Pranav Singhvi, Partner and Co-founder of CVF, General Catalyst. “When Otter enables enterprises to capture critical voice data and turns it into actionable business insights, teams move faster, decisions get sharper, and productivity compounds across the organization, and that’s why it’s a strong partner for CVF.”
There is a lot of competition in the market with well-funded meeting notetakers like Fireflies.ai,
Granola
, and
Read AI
; new entrants like
Calendly
,
Wispr
, and
Superhuman, which acquired Fathom
; and other notetakers like Circleback, Talat, and Quill.
Most of these notetakers want to connect to enterprise systems and, based on data captured in meetings, automate workflows. Otter is also heading in that direction. In the last few years, it introduced
a meeting assistant
,
a search function that works across apps
, and
integration with other AI tools
.
Otter’s newly appointed CMO, Alex Gay, who comes from Superhuman, told TechCrunch at a sit-down at the HumanX conference last month that the company sees a big opportunity in turning transcripts into an actionable roadmap for people who are in back-to-back meetings.
“When we start thinking about what is actually the bigger problem that people are facing right now, we saw this large pain point in meeting-heavy roles, where people are back-to-back in conversations. These meetings are the work for them. That’s either customer conversations or, from a sales standpoint. That’s where strategies are discussed. But meetings are terribly inefficient because when you come into a meeting, you spend the first twenty minutes recapping what was said before to catch everybody up,” he said.
The company is now experimenting with providing insights before, after, and during meetings. It has been testing a feature to send a pre-brief to users with details and background information, with context from previous conversations across surfaces. Plus, it is also trying out a Live Assist feature to let users ask questions to the AI assistant during the meeting to get knowledge.

articles.title: Yelp can now call on your behalf to check wait times at a restaurant
articles.summary: Yelp is embedding numerous new AI features into its app that can do everything from call to check on restaurant wait times to create personalized recommendations that remember your preferences.
articles.content:
Over the last few weeks, personal assistants like Instinct, Fo, and Muse have enabled users to call businesses for customer support and appointment booking. Following this trend, Yelp is adding the ability for its app users to get a voice agent to call a restaurant to check wait times.
The new feature, Check for Me, will show up on restaurant pages in the app, where users can enter their party size and phone number. The AI agent then calls on behalf of the user to check wait times and texts them the results to decide if they want to go to that particular restaurant.
Last year, Yelp debuted its
voice solution for restaurants and service providers
. With this new feature, the discovery platform is fulfilling the consumer side of the equation, though there is a possibility that a user’s agent will talk to the restaurant’s agent, and agent-to-agent communication might break down the conversation.

Image Credits:
Yelp
The company is also updating its Yelp AI assistant that helps users discover restaurants and services. With the new OpenTable integration, users can easily book a restaurant without leaving the app.
Yelp is adding better personalization to its assistant by having it remember preferences that you might have mentioned in previous chats. Plus, you can access your chat history from the past 30 days in the app, with full history available soon.
Users can ask the chatbot to set custom reminders, such as sending suggestions for weekend activities every Friday. The company is also letting users build their own lists, starting with two “Been Here” and “Want to
Go” lists. You can filter your lists by location, category, and cuisine, reorder, add notes to items, and share them with others.
Next month, the company will start showing weekly personalized recommendations based on your saved items and rankings. Yelp is also working on converting collections to lists and giving the lists tab a new look, rolling out later in the year, along with a maps view.

customer support
and
business processes
through AI. In the new update, the company is releasing a new paid product called Smart Lead Reply, which can reply to customers and engage with them to qualify a lead. Business owners, who will be charged $30 per month for these services, can specify how an agent should handle a conversation with a customer. AI offerings to handle inbound customer inquiries

articles.title: Mamdani says feds have abdicated on AI, urges New Yorkers to push back
articles.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Monday night that New Yorkers must resist the narrative that an AI takeover is inevitable and demand regulations that protect the public and put power back in their hands.
articles.content:
Two of New York’s sweethearts, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and activist and “Broad City” star Ilana Glazer, spoke about AI at Webster Hall in Manhattan on Monday night, with Glazer posing questions to the mayor about the future of AI in society.
Mamdani encouraged New Yorkers to resist the overwhelming feeling that AI is inevitably coming for their jobs, their kids’ minds, and their dignity, and to take back control instead.
His message came at a moment when the federal government is doing little to regulate AI, leaving cities to act on their own. At The People’s AI Assembly, an event hosted by the
AI Now Institute
, a think tank that explores the social implications of AI, Mamdani argued that the technology’s rapid rollout is not inevitable and that public officials should hold AI companies accountable.
Last month, Mamdani ordered a
ban on AI use
in elementary and middle schools. Glazer, a parent, said the technology’s arrival in classrooms unsettles her.
“It just makes me nervous. It feels so non-consensual, as though…this
has
to be in schools. It wasn’t two years ago. Why does it have to be in schools?” she said.
Over the summer, the mayor also introduced a policy that would require landlords, brokers, and real estate platforms to clearly disclose when a property’s listing photos or videos are made with AI. The policy is aimed at protecting New Yorkers from getting
“house-phished,”
or tricked by misleading listings.
Both moves challenge the assumption that schools and the public must simply accept AI as it arrives.
“Nothing
has
to be,” Mamdani said at the event Monday. “There’s a creep that comes with this, and there’s an intent to overwhelm that leaves people feeling as if there is simply no option.”
He said there has been a “reckless adoption of technology without any kind of a reckoning with the limitations of that technology,” citing the U.S. military’s February strike on a school in Iran that killed more than 150 people, including at least
123 children
. Officials involved in the Pentagon’s internal investigation have told Bloomberg that overreliance on AI in targeting was one factor in the attack.
“There is this desire to speak about [AI] as if it is infallible, as if it cannot be questioned, as if the only people who can regulate it are the ones who are currently developing it,” Mamdani said, noting that Facebook made similar arguments back in 2008. “What it really is,’ he continued, “is an attempt to escape any kind of accountability at any level, without also jeopardizing the potential valuation from an IPO.”
Anthropic is expected to debut on the public markets this year, and OpenAI has said it will go public in 2027.
Mamdani criticized the “complete abdication of federal law” when it comes to AI.
“At a national level, when the conversation is about artificial intelligence, it’s so often framed in this language of an arms race with China, and any of the humanistic concern, we just push to the side in a language of national competition,” the mayor said.
President Donald Trump’s
Superintelligence Task Force
, announced earlier this month, largely focuses on allowing powerful AI companies to self-regulate, rather than creating new federal restrictions. That comes despite growing fears about AI’s effect on every facet of human life, including warnings from whistleblowers at Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI that AI could lead to human extinction.
“As we are looking at what comes after this federal administration, there has to be a very different kind of framework in how we think about AI, talk about AI, the accountability we’re willing to bring forward when it comes to that,” Mamdani said.

articles.title: DeepInfer: High-performance inference framework for DeepSeek models
articles.content:
Title: GitHub - deepseek-ai/DeepInfer: DeepInfer: High-performance, large-scale inference framework for DeepSeek models

URL Source: https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer

Markdown Content:
DeepInfer is the high-performance inference framework that powers DeepSeek's large-scale production services. This open-source release provides offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale.

Supported models:

*   DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Supported features:

*   Optimized kernels, model and sampler runtime
*   Parallelism: Attention DP / balanced CP, MoE EP + EPLB
*   DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification
*   SWA bounded replay
*   Asynchronous scheduling (zero-overhead batch scheduler)
*   Batch-invariant inference
*   Deterministic sampling
*   Structured outputs

Feature details and configuration
*   **Optimized kernels:**[FlashMLA](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/FlashMLA), [DeepGEMM](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM), [DeepEP](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP), [TileKernels](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/TileKernels), [DeepSelect](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSelect), and custom [TileLang kernels](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/deepinfer/model_executor/layers/tilelang_ops).
*   **DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification:** accelerate decoding with draft tokens and use confidence estimates to schedule verification. Set `DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1`; `DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE` controls the maximum draft length (default: 5).
*   **Decoder SWA bounded replay:** reduce decoder prefill work by replaying only a bounded suffix. Set `DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact` and `DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140` for the default V4.1 settings; the retained suffix must cover the SWA window plus the maximum backtracking length.
*   **Asynchronous scheduling:** overlap CPU batch scheduling with device execution. Enabled by default.
*   **Batch-invariant inference:** keep model results identical across different batch compositions. Enable with `DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` (NVIDIA only).
*   **Deterministic sampling:** produce identical outputs for identical input tokens and sampling parameters. Set `DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0` and pass a fixed `seq_seed` to `SamplingParams` (NVIDIA only).
*   **Structured outputs:** constrain generation to a regex, JSON schema, or EBNF grammar. Pass `so_args={"schema_type": ..., "schema": ...}` to `SamplingParams`; see [examples](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/examples/_structured_output.py).

Supported hardware:

*   NVIDIA SM100 GPUs
*   Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs

Required for a complete inference service (not included in this release):

*   A KV cache system
*   VE/Prefill/Decode disaggregation (most required engine functionality is already implemented)
*   Load balancing across data-parallel replicas for both prefill and decode

## Getting started

### Prerequisites

*   Linux
*   GCC >= 13.0
*   Python 3.12
*   CUDA 13 (NVIDIA only)
*   CANN 9.2 (Ascend only)

articles.content:
Title: Publish stats, get cited: The tactic that put my data all over the web

URL Source: https://peec.ai/blog/publish-stats-get-cited-the-tactic-that-put-my-data-all-over-the-web

Published Time: 2026-10-07T12:41:00.085Z

Markdown Content:
_What I learned about AI search when I made up 50,000 stats that got cited by ChatGPT..._

About 7 months ago, I launched a website with 50,000 statistics. Every one of them was fake.

Google has forgotten the site exists and deindexed the pages, but ChatGPT hasn't. Since the website went live 7 months ago, it has sent more than 10,000 AI sessions its way. And now more than 330 referring domains, including Shopify, Bluehost, and DHL, link to the site. Its made-up numbers have also ended up in an academic paper and in a bank's investment research.

At Peec AI and in the industry, we talk about GEO and SEO every day, and we keep looking for new tactics. I’ve been working on this stats page one for a long time, sharing pieces of it publicly along the way. Of course, it’s experimental, but the results have been hard to ignore.

## Where the idea for publishing fake statistics came from

The impetus to seed a site with statistics came out of long-running research I've been doing on LLMs, relevance engineering, and grounding (credit to the iPullRank team, Dan Petrovic, and Wil Reynolds).

In the course of my work, I noticed a pattern: as more teams write time-sensitive and breaking content with LLMs, those LLMs have to look for (seemingly) reliable data during their research to fill the gaps in their knowledge. Statistics are often exactly what they’re looking for.

Most GEO advice focuses on one moment: getting your brand into the AI answer. This experiment looks at what happens after the answer, when people take that output and use it, putting it into presentations, adding it to a shopping list, and yes, publishing it on their website.

I didn't come up with the idea for this experiment alone. Hat tip to Seer Interactive, who already published [an eye-opening study](https://www.seerinteractive.com/insights/ai-optimization-test-footers-are-back-like-2003) in August 2025 that got a few thoughts bouncing around in my head. Several months later, those thoughts came together and finally made it to the top of my to-do list. In March 2026, I started working on building the site that would let me test my ideas.

## The setup: a website and 50,000 made-up stats, created in one day

Quick context for anyone who wasn’t following along in real time as I ran this experiment:

I bought a brand-new domain, stateglobe.com, and generated 50,000 statistics pages in a single day with GPT-4.1. The site purports to provide stats on SEO, content marketing, social media, e-commerce, and web technology from 200 countries. Except every number was totally invented. I never checked a single one. I pushed them to the site with a basic AI web design template. This cost me around $30. Later, I added 15,000 listicles on top of the statistics. That was about $20 more, so all in all, this is an experiment that came in at the very low price of about $50.

The reaction when I first shared it was wild. When my friend Kevin featured it in [Growth Memo](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/growth-intelligence-brief-15), it reached a much bigger audience. I think people responded so enthusiastically to this work because it showed great results while also speaking to the fears people have about what ends up in AI search results.

## What happened

1.   ### Google buried the site almost immediately

When I launched the site, traffic, indexing, and engagement were initially going really well. Using indexer tools, I got almost the entire site indexed within a week, and it started to appear in Google results.

Then two Google updates came out right after launch, and my Google visibility collapsed.

I've been invisible on Google for many months now. Indexed pages bounce between 5 and 20 impressions. At one point, I got curious and created a subdomain to see if I could increase impressions, but it didn't really help.

Other than that, I haven't touched the site. Some pages might even fail to load now and then. I don't know.

But when I sat down to write this, I checked the crawl data in Cloudflare after 7 months.

In the last 30 days alone, the site got more than 600,000 requests from bots. Around 72,000 of them came from ChatGPT-User. That is the agent ChatGPT uses to open a page in real time while answering someone. So these are not training crawls. Each one is ChatGPT fetching a fake statistics page to answer a real question.

1.   ### Unlike Google, ChatGPT never stopped pulling from the site

And when I say, “never stopped,” I mean ChatGPT _really_ never stopped.

**After 7 months, the site now has 330+ referring domains**

According to Ahrefs and Semrush, the site has links from 330+ other sites. That includes well-known brands like Shopify, DHL, and Bluehost. With strong Google performance, the numbers might have been even better.

**ChatGPT is still citing it to this day**

Google may have forgotten about the site, but ChatGPT clearly hasn’t. The site is still earning citations and traffic more than 7 months after launch.

_If you've read Tomek's_[_ChatGPT Index research_](https://peec.ai/blog/chatgpt-built-its-own-search-index)_, you're lucky, because it’s a great intro to how ChatGPT search works. If you haven't, add it to your reading list right now, because it helps explain why my website has been living in ChatGPT/OpenAI Index for so long._

A completely made-up website still performing so well is shocking. Since March, GA4 shows 10,000+ sessions from ChatGPT alone, and Cloudflare shows the site has high marks for retrieval.

_I didn’t include direct sessions in overall visits, because it mostly looks like bot traffic. Remember the dead internet theory!_

Right after I joined Peec in June 2026, I also set up a visibility dashboard in our tool to track a few prompts. Performance for them is still strong. On October 7, [stateglobe.com](http://stateglobe.com/) was ranked second for visibility on these prompts, behind only data powerhouse Statista.

**Retrieval is not ranking**

The constant retrieval is the first big lesson: ranking on Google and being retrievable by an LLM are two different problems.

When ChatGPT searches, it doesn't just copy Google's top 10. It rewrites your prompt into its own sub-queries (called fanout queries), pulls candidates from its search sources and its own cache, reranks them, and then opens a handful of pages to ground the answer. A page can be invisible on Google and still perform well in every one of those LLM steps.

StateGlobe is a good example. While Google dropped it, the AI retrieval bots kept coming back.

For GEO, this means Google rankings are only one signal, not the whole picture. If you only track Google, you are missing a channel that can work even when Google says “no.”

1.   ### Fake data turned into real citations

You’d expect that if a site performs well with information retrieval tools, its information would begin to appear out in the wild. And you would be right.

StateGlobe was built entirely on fake data, using the cheapest model available and a prompt that was nothing more than a list of countries and topics plus two sentences. Nevertheless, the output was…

…cited in an academic paper…

…used in investment research by Qatar's largest financial group…

…cited by an economics publication in India…

…and used as a source in a research report from a Canadian influencer community.

Note that these are only the citations that linked back to the StateGlobe site. Presumably, many more used the data without a link.

**The uncomfortable implication: citation laundering**

On day one, a fake number on StateGlobe had zero authority. It was a random stat on a brand-new domain.

Then an academic paper cited it. Then a bank. Now the next person, or the next model, that finds this number sees a stat with a source. And that source is cited by serious institutions.

The fake data certainly didn't become true, but every citation made it look more trustworthy.

It has the potential to get worse: after so much retrieval and citation, these pages end up in web crawls, and web crawls end up in training data (I hope it hasn’t!). A number that started as a GPT-4.1 guess can become something the next model "knows."

This points to the larger risk suggested by this experiment, and it's why I'm sharing this as research, not as a playbook for fake content. Verifying sources should become an essential part of writers’ and researchers’ workflows.

1.   ### Lastly, we tried running our experiment with real data

Once I began working at Peec, I decided to try a version of this test again. As the GEO Research team, we talked through the results up until that point and quickly launched a simple new page. This time, there were no made-up numbers, and we checked every stat and properly cited its source. You can view it here: [peec.ai/ai-search-geo-statistics](https://peec.ai/ai-search-geo-statistics).

Almost immediately, sites we suspect use AI to write their content started linking to us. For the second time, using a second site, earning links by publishing statistical content proved that a hypothetically strong tactic worked in reality.

## Lessons learned

### Why publishing statistics leads to LLM citations

The two tests show that LLMs have a strong preference for seeking out statistics when asked to write articles. The mechanism is simple:

1.   More and more content is written with LLMs.

2.   When an LLM writes, it researches the appropriate topic.

3.   When the LLM hits a gap, it looks for a number to fill it.

The reasons behind this process are equally clear.

**Research means fanout queries asking for statistics**

When a prompt requires research, the model breaks it into sub-queries, adds modifiers like "statistics," "data," "report," or the current year (if also requested in the prompt text). If someone asks for the model to compose a blog post about remote work, the model will search for "remote work statistics 2026." Pages that optimize for what models search rather than for what humans type will appear more often in LLM results.

**A number looks like evidence that can fill knowledge gaps**

When a model is asked to draft a piece of writing, a citation to a page that says "Remote work is growing" adds little authority and remains vague. If that page instead says "X% of employees work remotely at least once a week," there’s suddenly something that is specific, quotable, and additive. When a model grounds an answer, a specific number is the most useful thing it can find. These numbers look like evidence, though as this experiment proves, sometimes they aren’t.

**The model doesn’t check the number**

A search-grounded piece of LLM-written content has a tight budget for latency and cost. The system fetches a few pages, pulls the relevant passages, and starts to write. Fact-checking doesn’t happen anywhere in the process.

Verifying a single statistic would mean finding independent sources, comparing them, and resolving conflicts. Across billions of prompts by millions of users, the costs in both time and money would add up, making verification too slow and too expensive for practical purposes.

To get around this, LLMs use rerankers that score relevance, but not truth. That means if a passage matches the query and looks authoritative, it gets used.

**Statistics have a built-in freshness that models like**

I've written before about [ChatGPT's recency bias](https://metehan.ai/blog/i-found-it-in-the-code-science-proved-it-in-the-lab-the-recency-bias-thats-reshaping-ai-search/) in how it scores sources. Statistics pages contain the year in the title, the headings, and the URL. Three built-in signals to the model that what’s on the page is fresh.

### How to build a statistics page the right way

Title: NixOS is making me less afraid

URL Source: https://entropicthoughts.com/nixos-is-making-me-less-afraid

Markdown Content:
Something funny happened a little while ago: I read about FreshRSS, and it sounded nice, so I _installed it on a server and started using it_. That would not have happened a year ago, but then again, a year ago I didn’t have any NixOS servers.

* * *

For the past few years, my rss feeds have lived locally on my phone only. There was a good idea behind that 1 1 I can mostly take time to read when I’m away from my computer anyway., but it never quite worked in practice. For one, many things are easier to read on a larger screen. But it was also brittle to trust a phone app to manage the read/unread status of thousands of articles across a hundred feeds.2 2 In particular, when I switched to a different phone I could migrate all feeds to it, but the read/unread status was lost along the way. What I really wanted was a server-side feed aggregator. This is software that runs on a server, manages rss feeds, and then I can read the rss feeds either through a web interface, or through client applications. I’ve wanted that for a while, but I’ve never taken the step, because it would be yet another side project to maintain the deployment of.

But now, with some NixOS experience, adding a working FreshRSS configuration (including backups) took 9 lines of Nix code 3 3 Plus a dozen more lines for the nginx reverse proxy configuration. It got a little complicated because I wanted to `proxy_pass` from a specific location block which required rewriting cookie paths. But that’s a me problem, not a NixOS problem.. That installation has just hands-off worked for the past few months. If or when that server breaks, I can spin up a new one running the exact same configuration, probably in something like 15 minutes. When we can do something like that, there is literally no reason to not just try the new software.

Contrast this against how FreshRSS is installed outside of NixOS. Then we’d

1.   download and extract an archive to the right location;
2.   configure permissions according to instructions;
3.   install nginx and php-fpm with necessary extra dependencies to the server;
4.   configure php-fpm pools and make nginx pass requests through to php-fpm;
5.   set up Let’s Encrypt certificates;
6.   set up backups; and
7.   hopefully remember how to do all the above if something breaks and we need to reinstall FreshRSS on a new or upgraded server later.

Of course, the FreshRSS project provides a container image which would shorten the process a little bit. It purports to set up Apache with mod_php and configure them the right way. Then we’d only need to configure backups, create a systemd service that runs the container, and manage nginx as a tls terminating reverse proxy in front of that, because the container image reasonably does not come with tls support. This is still stuff to remember, and there’s also no guarantee the same thing works six months down the line when reinstalling, unless we wrote down which exact container image we downloaded.4 4 It does not help to build the container image from source, because two builds from the same Dockerfile separated by time can result in rather different container images.

* * *

I have mentioned before how much I dislike maintaining side projects. That includes my own code, but also self-hosted services developed by someone else. I’m okay with a few minutes of maintenance here and there, but having to schedule hours of uninterrupted work to upgrade something, or spending _any_ amount of time at all on emergency maintenance, really kills my desire to work with computers.

You’d think someone of my disposition would be deep into configuration management, container orchestration, or both, but no. I have made honest attempts with CFEngine, Ansible, podman, and k3s but none of them improved my installation/configuration/deployment experience significantly over (a) carefully writing things down, and sometimes (b) turning those careful notes into a shell script performing a sequence of `ssh` commands.5 5 Yes, this is essentially reinventing Ansible – but less brittle. It won’t break the next time someone glances sideways at `pip`. The drawback of the shell script is that it often ends up relying on assumptions that become invalid with time, or when it is used in a different environment. A NixOS configuration reads a lot like the careful instructions to myself, except they’re executable and they produce the same result every time.
